segments.translit: prajñāpāramitāmbhodhiparimathanatvāmṛtaparisnapitaḥ siddhācāryya bhusupādo vaṅgālikāvyājena tam evārthaṃ pratipādayati—
segments.translation: Bathed all over in the [nectar]{amrta} from churning the ocean of the [perfection of wisdom]{prajnaparamita}, the [siddha]{siddha} master [Bhusukupāda]{p-bhusuku} sets forth that same meaning under the guise of a [Bengali]{bangali} woman:
segments.note: Munidatta introduces the song: Bhusukupāda, bathed in nectar from churning the ocean of the perfection of wisdom (an image from the myth of the ocean churned for the drink of immortality), sets forth the same meaning under the guise of a Bengali woman (vaṅgālikā) (cp.49.m1).

flags.note: The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has de kho na nyid kyi bdud rtsis yongs su tshim pa, 'sated with the nectar of reality'. It points to -tattvāmṛta- where Shastri prints -parimathanatvāmṛta-, whose -tva- is ungrammatical (probably tattva with a syllable lost), and to a word for 'sated' (paritṛpta or parituṣṭa) where the Sanskrit has parisnapita, 'bathed all over'. I translate Shastri's text and leave the stray -tva- aside; with the Tibetan it would read 'sated with the nectar of reality churned from the ocean of the perfection of wisdom'.

For vaṅgālikāvyājena, 'under the guise of a Bengali woman', the Tibetan has nang 'khrug gi dgongs pa'i skad kyis, 'in the intentional language of inner strife': it takes the guise as intentional (twilight) language, and renders vaṅgālikā nang 'khrug, as it renders baṅgālī in its line 2a and Munidatta's vaṅgālikā and advayavaṅgāla (cp.49.m3, cp.49.m6). In its line 1b and in cp.49.m2 it instead transcribes Baṅgāla as a place (baM ga la).

vaṅgālikā is feminine, hence 'a Bengali woman'. It echoes the refrain's baṅgālī bhailī, which Munidatta renders with the feminine vaṅgālikā bhūtā (cp.49.m3). If the feminine only copies the song's form, 'a Bengali' would do.
The manuscript has the short form bhusupādo; I give the glossary form Bhusukupāda. The Tibetan has the full name, b+hu su ku'i zhabs.
The Tibetan renders tam evārthaṃ, 'that same meaning', as de kho na nyid kyi don, 'the meaning of reality', as if reading tattvārtham; it does the same in cp.49.m3.

segments.translit:
prajñāravindakuharahrade sadgurucaraṇopāyena praveśitaṃ | tatrānandādi śabdohītyādi akṣarasukhādvayavaṅgālena vāhita iti | abhinnatvaṃ kṛtam |
tathā cāgamaḥ—
na kleśā bodhito bhinna[ā] na bodhau kleśasambhavaḥ |
bhrāntitaḥ kleśasaṅkalpo bhrāntiḥ prakṛtinirmmalā ||
segments.translation:
It has been made to enter the [lake]{lake} in the hollow of the [lotus]{lotus} of [wisdom]{prajna}, by the [means]{upaya} of the true [guru]{guru}’s feet. There, ‘by the sound of joy and the rest’ and so on: it ‘was rowed’ by [imperishable bliss]{aksara-sukha}, the [nondual]{advaya} [Baṅgāla]{pl-bangala}. [Nondifference]{abheda} has been brought about. And so [scripture]{agama} says:
‘[Afflictions]{klesa} are not different from [awakening]{bodhi}, nor do afflictions arise in awakening.
The [conceptual thought]{vikalpa} of afflictions comes from [confusion]{bhranti}; confusion is stainless by nature.’
segments.note: Munidatta's paraphrase puts a lake in the hollow of the lotus of wisdom, entered through the true guru's feet, where the song has the lotus canal, and has 'it' rowed by Baṅgāla, which is nondual imperishable bliss; he names no boat. Nondifference, he says, is brought about, and he quotes scripture: afflictions are not different from awakening (cp.49.m2).

equations.en: rowed by Baṅgāla, which is imperishable bliss and nondual (the three set in apposition)

citations.quoted: na kleśā bodhito bhinnā na bodhau kleśasambhavaḥ | bhrāntitaḥ kleśasaṅkalpo bhrāntiḥ prakṛtinirmalā

flags.note: tatrānandādi śavdohītyādi is unclear and probably corrupt. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has de la dga' ba la sogs pa'i sgras zhes bya ba la sogs pa, 'There, “by the sound (or word) of joy and the rest,” and so on', as if reading ānandādiśabdena ityādi; I follow it. The words are not in the song as printed. A guess: Munidatta (cp.49.m2) takes the song's bāja as 'sound, music' (compare Bengali bājā, 'to sound'), where the draft reads vajra and the Tibetan line has rgyal po'i gru, 'the king's boat'.

Munidatta names neither the boat nor the vajra (cp.49.m2): what is 'made to enter' (praveśitaṃ, neuter) and what is 'rowed' (vāhitaḥ, masculine) have no stated subject. The vajra (bāja; Sanskrit vajra is masculine or neuter) entering the lotus would fit the union imagery he uses elsewhere, but that is my conjecture, so the note does not say it. His lake stands where the song has the lotus canal, with no explicit gloss.

The Tibetan comment has no lake: shes rab kyi chu skyes kyi sgo'i bu gar bla ma dam pa'i zhabs kyi thabs kyis rab tu 'jug go, '(it) enters into the opening of the door of the lotus of wisdom by the means of the true guru's feet', perhaps reading a word for 'door' where the Sanskrit has hrada, 'lake', and an intransitive 'enters' for the causative praveśitaṃ.

Baṅgāla: the Sanskrit is instrumental, 'rowed by the Vaṅgāla that is nondual imperishable bliss' (akṣarasukhādvayavaṅgālena vāhita). The Tibetan comment makes it a destination: mi 'gyur ba'i bde ba gnyis su med pa ni baM ga lar 'bab pa zhes te, 'unchanging nondual bliss is what is called “flowing down into Baṃgala”', reading vāhita as 'flowing' ('bab pa, as in its line 1a). Here and in its line 1b (baM ga la yul, 'the land of Baṃgala') the Tibetan treats Baṅgāla as a place; elsewhere it renders the word nang 'khrug, 'inner strife' (line 2a; cp.49.m1, cp.49.m3, cp.49.m6).

advaya: Munidatta reads the song's adaa as advaya, 'nondual' (akṣarasukhādvaya-, cp.49.m2; advayavaṅgāla, cp.49.m6), and the draft's 'nondual Baṅgāla' follows him. The Tibetan line of 1b has instead brtse ba med pas baM ga la yul khyer, 'pitilessly (or: the pitiless one) carried off the land of Baṃgala', as if reading adaya, 'merciless'; the Tibetan comment has gnyis su med pa, 'nondual', with Munidatta. The Tibetan line also has no word for the afflictions.

'Nondifference has been brought about' (abhinnatvaṃ kṛtam) and the verse after it seem to be Munidatta's reading of 'affliction was plundered' (kleśa luṛiu): the afflictions are made not different from awakening. He does not cite luṛiu, so the link is implied, not stated (cp.49.m2).

In the verse the Tibetan has byang chub nyon mongs las byung min, 'awakening does not arise from afflictions', where the Sanskrit says afflictions do not arise in awakening (na bodhau kleśasambhavaḥ). Shastri restores the final ā of bhinnā.

segments.translit:
dhruvapadena tam evārtham abhidyotayati |
ājītyādi | svayam evātmānaṃ sambodhya vadati | bho bhusukupāda dhyānaparipākāvasthāviyogenādyaiva vaṅgālikā bhūtā | yasmāt nijagṛhiṇī hy apariśuddhāvadhūtī vāyurūpā | caṇḍāleneti | sparśaprakṛtiprabhāsvareṇa nītā |
segments.translation: With the [refrain]{dhruvapada} he illuminates that same meaning. ‘Today’ and so on: he speaks addressing himself. ‘O [Bhusukupāda]{p-bhusuku}, through separation in the state in which [concentration]{dhyana} has ripened, today itself you have become a [Bengali]{bangali} woman.’ For his own [wife]{grhini} is the unpurified [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}, in the form of [wind]{vayu}. ‘By the [Caṇḍāla]{candala}’: she has been led away by touch, the natural [clear light]{prabhasvara}.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the refrain as Bhusukupāda addressing himself: through separation in the state of ripened concentration he has today become a Bengali woman, for his own wife, the unpurified avadhūtī (central channel) in the form of wind, has been led away by the Caṇḍāla, which he glosses as touch, the natural clear light (cp.49.m3).

equations.en: the unpurified avadhūtī, in the form of wind
touch, the natural clear light (sparśaprakṛtiprabhāsvara), by which the wife is led away

flags.note: Munidatta takes the refrain as self-address: 'he speaks addressing himself: O Bhusukupāda, … you have become' (cp.49.m3), so the song's bhūsu would be a vocative and bhailī second person. The draft's 2a is third person ('Bhusuku has become'). The Tibetan comment agrees with Munidatta (bdag nyid rang la yang dag par 'bod par gsungs te … kye'i b+hu su ku'i zhabs); the Tibetan line (de ring b+hu su ku pa nang 'khrug shor) does not decide it. Raised in questions.

dhyānaparipākāvasthāviyogena can mean 'through separation from the state in which concentration has ripened' or 'through separation in that state'. I follow the second, as the Tibetan does (bsam gtan yongs su smin pa'i gnas skabs na sbyor ba dang bral bas); the separation would then be the loss of the wife explained next (viyoga is the usual word for lovers' separation).

Where the Sanskrit has nijagṛhiṇī hy apariśuddhāvadhūtī vāyurūpā, 'his own wife is the unpurified avadhūtī, in the form of wind', the Tibetan has gang gi phyir nang gi khyim mi mo zhe na/ sems yongs su dag pa a wa d+hU tI ni rlung gi gzugs so, 'if you ask why: the inner wife; the fully purified mind, the avadhūtī, is the form of wind'. It lacks the negative (purified for unpurified), adds 'mind', and has 'inner' for nija, 'own'. The Sanskrit suits a wife who is led away; elsewhere Munidatta sets the purified avadhūtī (cp.02.m3) against the unpurified one (cp.10.m8).

sparśaprakṛtiprabhāsvareṇa: I read 'by touch, the natural clear light' (prakṛtiprabhāsvara is a compound Munidatta uses often); it can also be 'by the clear light whose nature is touch'. The Tibetan reg bya rang bzhin gyis 'od gsal gyis allows both. Why touch is named is unclear; a play on the Caṇḍāla as untouchable is possible (Munidatta says Ḍombī is so called because she cannot be touched, cp.10.m2), but he does not say so here (cp.49.m3).

Munidatta cites caṇḍālena, 'by the Caṇḍāla' (cp.49.m3), where Shastri's song has caṇḍālī (2b); the Tibetan line likewise has an agent, gtum pos khyer, 'carried off by the fierce one'. The draft follows them.

The Tibetan renders tam evārtham, 'that same meaning', as de kho na nyid kyi don, 'the meaning of reality', as in cp.49.m1, and vaṅgālikā bhūtā as nang 'khrug shor bar gyur pa, apparently 'inner strife has broken out'.

segments.translit:
dvitīyapadena bhāvaniḥsaṅgatām āha—
dahia ityādi | tena mahāsukhā[na]lena | pañcapāṭanam iti | pañcaskandhāśritāhaṃkāramamakārādikaṃ dagdhaṃ | indriyaviṣayañ ca | ataeva svayaṃ kalpaparihārān na jānīmaḥ cittaratnaṃ |
tathā ca sarahapādāḥ—
jathe tathevityādi—
segments.translation: With the second [verse]{pada} he speaks of nonattachment to things. ‘[Burned]{burning}’ and so on: by that fire of [great bliss]{mahasukha}. ‘[Pañcapāṭana]{pancadhata}’: [I-making and mine-making]{ahamkara-mamakara} and the like, resting on the five [aggregates]{skandha}, are burned, and the [senses]{indriya} and [sense objects]{visaya} too. Therefore, having ourselves given up [conceptual thought]{vikalpa}, we do not know the [mind-jewel]{citta-ratna}. And so [Saraha]{p-saraha} says: ‘Wherever …, there …’ and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta has the burning done by the fire of great bliss, and glosses pañcapāṭana, his form of the song's pañcadhāṭa, as I-making, mine-making and the like resting on the five aggregates, together with the senses and their objects. Having given up conceptions, 'we' do not know the mind-jewel; he points to a verse of Saraha (cp.49.m4).

equations.en: I-making, mine-making and the like, resting on the five aggregates, burned together with the senses and sense objects

citations.work: a verse of Saraha (Sarahapāda), whom Munidatta names; the verse itself is not identified

flags.note: Munidatta cites the first word of 3a as dahia, 'burned' (Sanskrit dagdha), where Shastri's song prints ḍahi (cp.49.m4). The Tibetan line and comment agree on burning (bsregs). The fire is his addition: the song names none. Shastri's restoration mahāsukhā[na]lena, 'by the fire of great bliss', is confirmed by the Tibetan bde ba chen po'i mes.

Munidatta cites the song's pañcadhāṭa as pañcapāṭana (cp.49.m4), whose own sense is no clearer (pāṭana, 'splitting'?). The Tibetan line and comment have rnam pa lnga po, 'the five kinds', which gives only the number. The draft keeps pañcadhāṭa in source form; the glossary's guess pañca ghāṭa, 'five landing places', gets no support from either witness.

ṇai and dibi saṃjñā: Munidatta has nothing that answers to a river (ṇai); in his gloss the five things themselves are burned. His 'and the senses and sense objects too' and 'having given up conceptual thought' may stand where the song has dibi saṃjñā ṇaṭhā, the second perhaps for saṃjñā ṇaṭhā, 'notions lost', but he gives no explicit gloss, and nothing in it points to 'divine perception' (cp.49.m4). The Tibetan line has yul rnams brlag, 'the objects destroyed', for the second half, and no river.

Munidatta's cittaratnaṃ, 'mind-jewel', paraphrases the song's cia mora, 'my mind', in 3b (cp.49.m4); the Tibetan line of 3b also has a jewel, rang sems rin chen, 'my own mind-jewel'. Both may reflect a song text with raaṇa, 'jewel'. The draft has 'my mind'.

The Tibetan renders bhāvaniḥsaṅgatā, 'nonattachment to things', as ngo bo nyid 'gyur ba med pa, 'unchanging nature'; it has phung po lnga las byung ba, 'arising from the five aggregates', for 'resting on' them, and rang gi rtog pa, 'one's own conceptual thought', for svayaṃ kalpa-.

Only the opening of Saraha's verse is cited, jathe tathe…, apparently Apabhraṃśa for 'where … there' (Sanskrit yatra … tatra); the Tibetan has ji ltar, 'as, how', as if for yathā. I have not identified the verse.

segments.translit:
tṛtīyapadena tam eva nirddiśati—
sona[ta]rua ityādi | sonam iti śūnyatāgrahaḥ | [ta]ruya iti bhāvagrahaḥ | ubhayavikalpaṃ svarūpavicāryyamāṇe sati kiñcin na sthitam | nijaparivāreṇeti | ataeva nirvvikalpaparihāreṇa mahāsukharatnanimagno 'haṃ |
tathā cāgamaḥ—
arthe(rthi)nā (ma)rthijanāna vināmatitarāṃ(?) dūraṃ nayantīha ye
dhanyās te nijabhoga(ge)saṅgamadhiyo dhyāyanti nakta[ṃ]dina[m] |
no paśyāmy aniśaṃ sukhāśrayapadaṃ dhyāyann ahaṃ mūḍhadhīḥ
sattvārthe(rtha) karuṇārase 'tigahane majjāmy akāṃkṣī punaḥ ||
segments.translation:
With the third [verse]{pada} he points out that same meaning. ‘Gold and silver’ and so on: ‘[gold]{gold}’ means grasping at [emptiness]{sunyata}; ‘[silver]{silver}’ means grasping at things. When the [conceptual thought]{vikalpa} of both comes under [examination]{vicara} of its [true nature]{svarupa}, nothing at all has remained. ‘With my own household’: therefore, through an abandonment free of concepts, I am immersed in the [jewel]{ratna} of [great bliss]{mahasukha}. And so [scripture]{agama} says:
‘Those who here, quite deliberately, send suppliants far off empty-handed,
fortunate are they, their minds set on union with their own pleasures: they meditate night and day.
I, a [fool]{mudha}, meditating without cease, do not see the state where [bliss]{sukha} rests;
for the sake of beings, wanting nothing, I sink again into the very deep flavour of [compassion]{karuna}.’
segments.note: Munidatta reads the gold as grasping at emptiness and the silver as grasping at things: examined in their true nature, both conceptions leave nothing. 'With my own household' he explains as being immersed in the jewel of great bliss through abandonment free of concepts, and he quotes a verse on sinking into compassion for beings (cp.49.m5).

citations.quoted: arthenārthijanān vinā matitarāṃ dūraṃ nayantīha ye / dhanyās te nijabhogasaṅgamadhiyo dhyāyanti naktaṃdinam / no paśyāmy aniśaṃ sukhāśrayapadaṃ dhyāyann ahaṃ mūḍhadhīḥ / sattvārthe karuṇārase ’tigahane majjāmy akāṅkṣī punaḥ

flags.note: Shastri restores [ta] in sona[ta]rua and [ta]ruya to match the song's soṇa tarua. The Tibetan comment transcribes so na and rU pa, the latter perhaps from rūpā, 'silver' (Old Bengali rūā?), and its line has gser dngul, 'gold, silver'. So the manuscript's sonarua and ruya may stand for sona rua, 'gold, silver', without the restoration (cp.49.m5). Either way Munidatta's pair is gold and silver, as in the draft.
For bhāvagrahaḥ, 'grasping at things', the Tibetan has gzung ba'i ngo bo, 'the nature of the grasped (object)'; for the gold it agrees, stong pa nyid 'dzin pa, 'grasping at emptiness'.

nirvikalpaparihāreṇa may mean 'through an abandonment free of concepts' (my rendering) or 'through giving up the nonconceptual', that is, even nonconceptuality. The Tibetan has de nyid las nges par rnam par rtog pa spangs pas, 'having decisively abandoned conceptual thought', as if taking nir- with the abandonment (cp.49.m5).

Munidatta paraphrases 'I remained in great bliss' (4b) as being immersed in 'the jewel of great bliss' (cp.49.m5); the Tibetan line of 4b also has a jewel, rang gi 'khor gyis rin chen blangs nas gnas, 'my own retinue took the jewel and stayed', where the Bengali has mahāsuhe. He does not gloss the household (parivāra; Tibetan 'khor, 'retinue').

The verse (śārdūlavikrīḍita metre) is corrupt and carries Shastri's queries. The metre allows line 1 to be read arthenārthijanān vinā matitarāṃ dūraṃ nayantīha ye, and requires nijabhoga- (not -bhoge-) in line 2. matitarām is doubtful; I render it 'quite deliberately'. The sense seems ironic: misers who turn suppliants away are 'fortunate' (dhanya, also 'wealthy'), while the speaker gives up his own bliss for beings.

The Tibetan of the verse differs: blo gros mchog gis, 'with supreme intelligence', for matitarām; rgyal ba'i longs spyod, 'the Victor's enjoyment', for nijabhoga- (reading jina for nija); nyin mi mthong, 'does not see the day'; and ma rig thibs por slar 'dod pa, 'longs again for the thick (darkness of) ignorance', for atigahane majjāmy akāṅkṣī punaḥ (reading kāṅkṣī, 'longing', without the negative).

segments.translit:
caturthapadenātyantābhāvam āha—
caukoṭītyādi | yat paraṃ catuṣkoṭivicārabhaṇḍāraṃ mama tena advayavaṅgālena gṛhītam | ataeva [ma]mātmani jīvaṇamaraṇadhyānādivikalpaṃ nāsti |
tathā ca hevajre—
pitari prāptaṃ yat saukhyam ityādi | 49 ||
segments.translation: With the fourth [verse]{pada} he speaks of [absolute nonexistence]{atyantabhava}. ‘[Four crores]{four-crores}’ and so on: my highest [storehouse]{storehouse}, that of [examination]{vicara} by the [four alternatives]{catuskoti}, has been taken by that [nondual]{advaya} [Baṅgāla]{pl-bangala}. Therefore in my self there is no [conceptual thought]{vikalpa} of [living]{jivanta} and dying, of [concentration]{dhyana} and the like. And so in the [Hevajra]{tx-hevajra}: ‘The bliss that is obtained in the father …’ and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta says the last couplet speaks of absolute nonexistence. He takes caukoṭī, 'four crores', as catuṣkoṭi, the four alternatives: his storehouse of examination by them has been taken by the nondual Baṅgāla, so he has no concepts of living, dying, meditation and the like. He points to a Hevajra verse (cp.49.m6).

equations.en: the storehouse of examination by the four alternatives (catuṣkoṭivicārabhaṇḍāra)

citations.quoted: pitari prāptaṃ yat saukhyam … (opening words only)
citations.work: Hevajra Tantra, named by Munidatta; the passage is not located

flags.note: For atyantābhāvam, 'absolute nonexistence', the Tibetan has shin tu bsgoms pa, 'thorough meditation', as if reading atyantabhāvanā (cp.49.m6).

Munidatta cites the song's caukoṛi as caukoṭī and takes it as catuṣkoṭi, the four alternatives (koṭi, 'point'), not four crores (koṭi, 'ten million') (cp.49.m6). The Tibetan line has bye ba phrag bzhi, 'four ten-millions'; the Tibetan comment cites those words but explains them with mtha' bzhi, 'the four extremes'. The draft keeps 'four crores' in the line.

yat paraṃ, 'what was highest', is gzhan gang, 'whatever other', in the Tibetan, and advayavaṅgālena, 'by the nondual Baṅgāla', becomes gnyis su med pas na nang 'khrug pa de yis, 'since it is nondual, by that one of inner strife'. Shastri's restoration [ma]mātmani is supported by the Tibetan bdag, 'I'.

The Hevajra is cited by its opening words only, pitari prāptaṃ yat saukhyam, 'the bliss that is obtained in the father'; the Tibetan has de yi bde ba nyid thob, 'the bliss of that is obtained', with no father. I have not located the verse in the tantra. The closing 49 is the song number, not translated.

questions: Refrain 2a: Munidatta reads it as self-address ('O Bhusukupāda, … you have become', cp.49.m3), and the Tibetan comment agrees; the draft has third person. Should 2a become something like 'Today, Bhusu, you have become a Bengali', or stay third person with a note on his reading?
Munidatta's vaṅgālikā is feminine (cp.49.m1, cp.49.m3), so I render 'a Bengali woman' in the commentary. Is that acceptable beside the draft's ungendered 'a Bengali' in 2a?

1a bāja: the draft reads 'vajra', the Tibetan line 'king' (rgyal po'i gru, 'the king's boat'), and Munidatta's garbled 'by the sound of joy and the rest' (cp.49.m2) might take it as 'sound, music'. Should 1a carry a reading flag?
1b adaa: the Tibetan line reads 'pitilessly' (brtse ba med pas, as if adaya), against Munidatta's advaya (cp.49.m2, cp.49.m6) and the draft's 'nondual'. Add a witness note on 1b?

Baṅgāla: the Tibetan transcribes it as a place in 1b and cp.49.m2 (baM ga la) but renders baṅgālī, vaṅgālikā and advayavaṅgāla as nang 'khrug, 'inner strife', in 2a, cp.49.m1, cp.49.m3 and cp.49.m6. Should the pl-bangala and bangali entries record both renderings?

3b and 4b: Munidatta (cittaratna, cp.49.m4; mahāsukharatna, cp.49.m5) and the Tibetan lines (rang sems rin chen; rin chen blangs) both have a jewel the Bengali lacks. Is that worth a witness note on 3b ('my mind') and 4b?

3a: Munidatta gives nothing for the river (ṇai) and nothing like 'divine perception' (dibi saṃjñā) (cp.49.m4), and the Tibetan line has 'the objects destroyed'. The draft's 'river' and 'divine perception' rest on the Bengali alone; should 3a be flagged?
Shastri's restored [ta] in sona[ta]rua (cp.49.m5): the Tibetan rU pa suggests the manuscript's sonarua may be sona rua, 'gold, silver', without the restoration. Note it on 4a, or only here?

Keep-source-first-gloss terms (siddha, avadhūtī, Caṇḍāla, pañcadhāṭa) first occur in this unit's commentary. I glossed avadhūtī briefly in the note to cp.49.m3 and left the other first-gloss notes to the song layer. Is that right for commentary segments?
The scripture verse in cp.49.m5 is corrupt; I translated a text regularized by the metre. Print the translation as it stands, or mark it as uncertain for readers?
